newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices seen strong at least through July.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices seen strong at least through July.

text.p: Coffee prices extended their stunning rally Thursday to new 20-year highs and analysts said low inventories combined with the onset of Brazil's winter months could keep the bull market running for at least another two months.
The July coffee contract closed up 19.25 cents at $3.148 a pound on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange. It was the first time in two decades that coffee traded above $3 a pound.
The rally is unprecedented in that there has not -- yet -- been a winter frost in Brazil this year.
"Who is going to short (sell) this market going into the (Brazilian) winter with tight supplies?" Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes said of weather fears in the largest coffee-growing country.
"If Brazil doesn't have a freeze, the speculators could go to the bank, but they will probably wait until mid-July," she said.

Worries that cold weather could damage coffee trees in Brazil typically fuels buying of coffee ahead of the country's June-through-August winter season. Brazil normally supplies at least a quarter of the world's coffee each year.

But coffee inventories in both consumer and producer nations have already fallen to 20-year lows, a situation that has sparked a five-month rally in coffee futures and several rounds of price hikes by big roasters such as Folgers, Nestle and Maxwell House.

Any signs of cool weather in Brazil sparked further frenzied buying this week. Traders' memories are still fresh of two severe frosts in June and July, 1994 that wiped out Brazil's coffee crop and sent world prices higher.

"Temperatures are becoming cooler and the fact that we're coming into the heart of the cold weather season with the low stock levels makes this rally more sustainable," said one coffee market analyst at the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange.
Futures prices have rocketed more than 150 percent since the beginning of the year, with prices now at levels not seen since the Spring of 1977.
"Speculators have been piling into coffee ahead of the frost season in Brazil," the brokerage GNI Ltd. said in a monthly report.

Should a severe frost hit Brazil, "then coffee prices could soar to $5, perhaps $7 per pound," it said. "But if a frost is not seen, the downside for prices could perhaps be $1.50 or so. It seems like a fair bet."

Supply worries have been cemented since January by forecasts of smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries, labour unrest in the two largest producers, Colombia and Brazil, and projections for a smaller crop in Brazil in the coming 1997/98 season, which starts next month.

Although Brazil is beginning to harvest its new-crop coffee, analysts said a lack of deliverable supplies of quality "arabica" or mild, washed coffee beans from Central America and Colombia ahead of harvests this autumn will also underpin prices.

"The perception is that supply is tight and will remain tight into the December contract," said Ann Prendergast, an analyst for Refco Inc. "I don't expect to see any enormous amount of coffee coming onto the market between now and October, and that's going to support prices."

While the futures market appears to be racing unopposed toward the all-time record futures price of $3.407 a pound set on April 14, 1977, some traders feared a consumer backlash in response to higher retail prices.

"This is an historic moment -- but also a worrying one. These prices could start to hit consumption as housewives may start buying smaller quantities," said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association.

Folgers and Maxwell House have already hiked prices on their 13-ounce can of regular ground coffee by nearly 50 percent, and traders said another rise -- the fifth in less than four months -- could be in store for coffee drinkers as soon as next week.
On Wednesday, Starbucks Corp. said it planned to raise prices for the second time this year to reflect the higher cost of coffee beans worldwide.
"It (higher prices) may take some time to affect consumption, but it will eat into it," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "People will try to economise and use less."
